segments.say: Get comfortable. Tonight, I'd like to talk about something that almost everyone does, and almost everyone feels a little bad about. Putting things off. That email you've been meaning to send for days. The project that's due next week. The phone call you keep postponing. Tonight, we're going to look at why we procrastinate.

And I want to promise you something right at the start. This won't be a lecture. Nobody is going to tell you to just try harder. Because the research on procrastination tells a much more interesting, and much kinder, story than that. Procrastination, it turns out, is not really about laziness at all.

Think about the last time you procrastinated. Were you being lazy? Or were you actually quite busy? Many people, when they put off an important task, find themselves suddenly cleaning the kitchen, answering easy emails, reorganizing a drawer. We're often very active while procrastinating. Just not on the thing we're supposed to do.

So what is procrastination, really? Psychologists often define it as voluntarily delaying an intended course of action, despite expecting to be worse off for the delay. In other words, we choose to delay something we intended to do, even though we know, deep down, that delaying it will probably make things harder.

That's a strange choice when you think about it. Why would anyone knowingly make their own life harder? That puzzle is what makes procrastination so fascinating. And researchers have been working on it for decades, from many different angles. Emotions, time, the brain, motivation, even evolution.

Here's where we're going tonight. First, how common procrastination really is. Then, why it's more about feelings than laziness. Why our future self can feel like a stranger. How deadlines and simple plans can help. And why, surprisingly, forgiving yourself may work much better than feeling guilty.
